title: Comment from Michigan Works! West Central

comment:
In response to 20 CFR Parts 684, 686, and 688, [Docket No. ETA–2022–0005], RIN 1205–AC08, Nevada would like to submit the following comments for consideration.

•Retention with the Same Employer was the least selected measure by the states during the pilot period. High housing costs and inflation cause people to change employers. High living costs have forced many workers to move from more expensive metropolitan areas to less expensive rural areas, thus leaving their employment. This is true for many states.
•Retention with the Same Employer is an unfavorable measure to determine effectiveness in serving employers due to the transient workforce that makes up most of Nevada. Nevada’s economy is evolving and so is our workforce. Nevada job seekers typically go through a series of poorly paying jobs, that do not need special skills, as they train for new careers with higher pay (i.e., retail to healthcare).
•While using the Retention with the Same Employer measure may be require less administrative costs, Nevada is concerned that meeting performance goals with this measure will be difficult, negating the administrative cost savings. In Nevada, workers change jobs for only slight pay increases. In this highly competitive job market workers can change jobs 2-3 times per year going to the employer with only minimally higher pay. As a result, using the Retention with the Same Employer measure is not an effective way of determining the effectiveness of Employer Services being provided. A possible alternate measure of retention within the same industry would be a better indicator.

Thank you for this opportunity to comment on DOL ETA’s Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act Title I Non-Core Programs Effectiveness in Serving Employers Performance Indicator proposed rule.

comment:
My comments do to indicate support or opposition to the proposed measure but rather concern how it will be applied. The Retention of Employment with the Same Employer measure is run as the Participant level which means it is available by program for each exiter who was employed in the second quarter after exit. My recommendation is that this measure be reported for each of the 6 core WIOA programs (Adult, DW, Youth, WP, AEFLA, VR) along with separate targets for each that reflect the unique factors influencing performance on this indicator. The reason for this recommendation is based on the Departments' Sanction Policy which provides 3 ways for a state to "fail" performance:

1) achieve less than 50% of target on any single measure
2) achieve less than an average of 90% of target across all measures in all programs
3) achieve less than an average of 90% of target across all programs in one measure

If Effectiveness in Serving Employers is only run at the "system" level with a single target, it means that under the 3rd listed criteria for failure, achieving less than 90% of target on this one measure, would be considered a failure and if it were repeated the next year, result in sanction. That is not consistent with the intent of the model that the Departments set up in their sanction policy whereby a state would only be considered to have failed on the basis of a single measure if they achieved <50% of target on that measure.

There is a practical reason for applying this measure to each of the 6 core programs separately: the Departments will have great difficulty creating a statistical model for a unified measure that accounts for those we serve, because the Department of Education does not get participant level data which will make it much harder to establish casemixes across the programs - and as we have seen in the existing statistical models, the model elements and weights can vary greatly across the programs, even on the same measure. And states do not have the same proportion of individuals served across the programs so to the degree that a state has dramatically different degrees of coenrollment or just natural differences in utilization of their programs, the models won't be able to easily address this.

If the Departments decide to proceed with a single measure applied to all 6 core programs using one statistical model applied at the system level, I would recommend that they amend their Sanctions Policy to specify that the criteria of achieving an average of <90% of target across one measure category not be applied to the Effectiveness in Serving Employers measure. The Departments' original design of the sanction policy was clearly intended to look for either catastrophic failures on a single measure (<50% of target) or systemic performance issues in a program or in a measure across programs (average of <90% of target). Applying the <90% standard to Effectiveness in Serving Employers simply because it is its own measurement category is not consistent with that original vision and is likely to result in significantly greater risk of sanction resulting from a measure that, while piloted by many states, has probably not really been focused on or analyzed to determine what state or its partners can do to improve outcomes.
title: Comment from Anonymous

comment:
The Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) concerning TEGL 10-16, Change 2 - Performance Accountability Guidance for Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Core Programs – concerning Effectiveness in Serving Employers (ESE) indicators under WIOA. The Department acknowledges the merit of measuring employer effectiveness in a dual-customer WIOA system and further acknowledges how difficult it is to identify an employer effectiveness measure that is reliable, representative, and easy to administer. Rhode Island tracked all three pilot measures during the trial performance period. We observed that each measure had their own strengths and weaknesses. We will address these, as well as our observations and concerns with selecting Retention with the Same Employer as the single ESE indicator, below:

• Employer penetration is useful as a measure of ‘brand awareness’ but is more an indicator of quantity, not quality/satisfaction. It’s also a lagging/secondary indicator in that if we are performing well for employers and they are ‘satisfied’ with our services; then our penetration rate should, in theory, increase.
• Repeat business customer is a bit more useful as measure but lacks context based on the industry and employer. In our experience, repeat business customers in WIOA are not that uncommon, but they may be more attracted to the financial benefit of programs like OJTs or IWT than satisfied with a particular outcome or service.
• Of all proposed/current or theoretical measures, Retention with Same Employer is the easiest for Rhode Island to administer and the most consistent to apply across WIOA programs.
• Retention also better indicates some level of employer satisfaction, or at least the absence of dissatisfaction, with the placement.
• However, retention does not speak to acuity of placement (for example; how difficult the position was to fill, how in-demand the position is, whether the role was seasonal specific and not intended to maintain retention, rarity of skill set, time to hire, etc.).
• Retention may not be the desired outcome for the job seeker, especially if the placement is in a lower wage position, nor does retention reflect whether the employee is required to work at more than one employer to maintain a living wage.
• Retention does not currently speak to what business service, if any, the employer received.
• Retention combined with some measure of acuity (skill/education level of the position, time to placement, etc.) and the ability to filter for those employers who received a business service, would improve the measure.

Again, the Department appreciates the opportunity to comment on the NPRM and would be happy to provide additional information and comment upon request.
title: Comment from Department of Labor and Training

comment:
As the Executive Director of a local workforce development board, and the head of an organization that delivers jobseeker and employer services, I disagree with using 2nd and 4th quarter retention with the same employer as a measure of effectiveness of employer services. Achieving this measure requires ongoing support of the jobseeker, not the employer. The measure is an employment retention measure, and achieving it requires effort on the part of both the jobseeker and the employer. Effort by the jobseeker could include support from the WIOA job counselor through follow-up services, which we normally provide. Effort on the part of the employer has to do with wage, working conditions, workplace culture, and other factors that aren't related to the employer services WIOA program staff provide. As a result, achievement of this performance target has little or no relation to WIOA employer services delivered. It also limits the jobseeker's movement from a lower-wage job to a higher-wage job, which is a disincentive for career advancement.

In contrast, the other two proposed measures do directly relate to WIOA employer services delivered. (2) Repeat Business Customer: Percentage of employers who have used WIOA core program services more than once during the last three reporting periods - this measure reflects the employer's perception or actual experience of the quality of services they received. If they return to become a continued partner of the workforce system, this implies they see value in our services. (3) Employer Penetration: Percentage of employers using WIOA core program services out of all employers in the State - this is also a better measure of the quality of employer services, though it would be harder to track as the definition of using WIOA core program services varies across states and entities. But it does represent the level of impact of employer services in a state, and can be subdivided to measure the impact of sector initiatives led by workforce boards and/or WIOA program staff. While on their own these two measures might generate negative outcomes (too much focus on a small group of employers, numbers rather than quality of services) combined they offer a better reflection of the effectiveness of employer services delivered.

comment: The fact that the Employment and Training Administration is proposing more rules in the Indian and Native American (INA) programs, the Job Corps program, the YouthBuild programs, and the National Farmworker Jobs Program (NFJP), while subsequently removing restrictions on migrant labor in the United States, boggles the mind. This proposed rule (1205-AC08) seeks to add another requirement (effectiveness in serving employers) to an already burdened list of requirements. Why is this requirement (effectiveness in serving employers) not evaluated against migrant laborers who do not have adequate, legal paperwork and thus cause more difficulty for their employers in the agricultural and meat spaces? Why is this requirement (effectiveness in serving employers) not evaluated for migrants pouring over the southern border (up to 2 million persons in 2022 alone!) who have criminal histories including attacks on women and children? United States workplaces are diverse and contain women. Shouldn't the Employment and Training Administration (ETA), Labor be concerned with who they are letting in workplaces, and not just whether employers are served effectively or not? Moreover, effectiveness in serving an employer could be measured a variety of ways and this rule fails to set out any objective standard. Effectiveness in serving an employer could relate to timeliness, professionalism or English proficiency. I dare the Employment and Training Administration (ETA), Labor to establish that all documents should be in English in this rule, and completed by U.S. citizens with zero criminal background and extensive English and professional records. I dare you to do that. That would satisfy this proposed rule, wouldn't it? It would, but it would fly in the face of this administration's decision to undermine the American worker in favor of foreign nationals. #RememberMarthasVineyard
